client: I just don't understand how I'm supposed to keep going through the motions anymore. Everything that used to make me happy - our favorite hiking trails, cooking meals we loved, even watching our shows - it all just feels empty now. People tell me time will help but six months have passed and I still feel like I'm just going through the motions, like part of me died in that accident too.
therapist:
I hear how deeply painful this loss still feels for you, and how the things that once brought joy now feel hollow. The way your voice catches as you describe this makes me wonder if part of you is still in shock about how much has changed. 

Would it help to talk about what it might look like to honor both your grief and the part of you that's still here, still trying to find meaning?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know how to honor anything right now. Some days I can barely get out of bed. People keep telling me I should be "grateful for the time we had" but that just makes me angry - like they don't understand this wasn't just some relationship, this was my whole life. 

The worst part is I still catch myself reaching for my phone to text her about little things throughout the day, and then it hits me all over again.
therapist:
It sounds like the pain of her absence keeps catching you unexpectedly, in those everyday moments when you'd normally share your thoughts with her. Your voice softens when you describe this, suggesting how tender and raw that grief still feels.

Would it be okay to explore together how we might create space for both honoring that deep connection and gradually finding ways to carry her memory forward in your life?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... I guess I'm scared that if I try to "carry her memory forward" it will feel like I'm moving on and leaving her behind. Everyone keeps telling me I need to start living again, but how do I do that without feeling like I'm betraying what we had? It's like I'm stuck between wanting to honor her and feeling like I'm supposed to get over this already.
therapist:
Your voice softens even more when you talk about this fear of betraying her memory, which tells me how deeply sacred this love still feels to you. There's such a painful tension between honoring what you had and facing the future without her.  

What if "moving forward" wasn't about leaving her behind, but about finding ways to keep her with you in new forms? Would it help to explore what that might look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... every time I try to imagine keeping her with me in new ways, it just feels like a cheap replacement. Like that time I tried watching our favorite show without her - I had to turn it off after 5 minutes. Maybe some losses just can't be transformed like that. 

But part of me is exhausted from carrying this pain every single day too. I just don't know how to hold both things at once.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between wanting to find new ways to honor her memory and worrying that it might diminish what you shared. The way you describe feeling exhausted from the weight of this pain suggests how much energy this grief has been taking from you.  

Perhaps we could explore together what it might look like to create small moments of rest from the pain, not as a replacement for her, but as a way to care for yourself while continuing to honor what you shared?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I could try that, but it feels selfish somehow. Like if I'm not in pain all the time, it means I didn't love her enough. I keep thinking about our last conversation before the accident - we were arguing about something stupid, and now I'll never get to fix it. That guilt keeps me from feeling like I deserve any rest.
therapist:
Your voice speeds up as you share about that last conversation, and I can hear how much that unfinished moment weighs on you. It's understandable to feel that pain so deeply, but I wonder if holding onto that guilt might be keeping you from honoring the many beautiful moments you shared together.  

Could we explore how you might balance acknowledging that difficult last interaction with celebrating the love that was present throughout your relationship?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I could try to focus on the good memories, but that last conversation keeps replaying in my head like a broken record. It's like no matter how many happy moments we had, that one argument overshadows everything else. 

Maybe it's because I never got to say I'm sorry or tell her how much she meant to me one last time. That's what haunts me the most - that she died thinking I was mad at her.
therapist:
It sounds like that unfinished moment holds so much pain for you, replaying in your mind as you wish for a chance to express your love and apology. While your words carry sadness, your voice sounds softer now, perhaps showing how much tenderness still surrounds your memories of her.

Would it be okay to explore what you might say to her now, if you could? Sometimes putting those feelings into words can help ease the weight of that unfinished conversation.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know... I've tried writing letters to her before, but it just makes me feel worse because I know she'll never read them. It feels pointless, like I'm just talking to myself. 

But I guess if I could say anything... I'd tell her I'm sorry for that stupid fight, and that she was the best thing that ever happened to me. I just wish I could hear her say she forgives me.
therapist:
The way your voice quiets when you share what you'd say to her tells me how much love still lives in those words, even through the pain. It's understandable that writing letters felt too painful before, but I hear something different in your voice now as you imagine telling her these things.  

What if forgiveness wasn't something you needed to hear from her, but something you could begin to offer yourself for being human in that last conversation? Would that feel possible to explore?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
That's... hard to even think about. I don't know if I deserve to forgive myself when she can't be here to say it's okay. But I also know she wouldn't want me beating myself up like this forever - she was always the first to say sorry after our fights. 

It just feels like if I let go of this guilt, I'm letting go of her too, and I'm not ready for that yet.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding onto that guilt as a way to stay connected to her, even while knowing she would likely want you to find peace. The way your voice rises when you talk about this suggests how much this conflict matters to you.  

What if forgiving yourself wasn't about letting go of her, but about honoring the love and forgiveness she would likely want for you? Could we explore how that might feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I never thought about it that way - that holding onto guilt might actually be going against what she would want for me. That makes me tear up just thinking about it. 

But it's so hard to imagine feeling okay when she's not here. Like if I stop punishing myself, I'm saying what happened was okay, and it wasn't okay at all.
therapist:
Your voice shakes as you share this realization, showing how deeply this idea touches you. It's understandable to feel conflicted - wanting to honor what happened while also recognizing that holding onto guilt might not be what she would have wanted.

Perhaps we could explore together how you might begin to honor her memory in ways that align with the love and compassion she showed you, rather than through pain and self-punishment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess I could try... but what would that even look like? Every time I think about doing something she would've liked - like donating to her favorite animal shelter or listening to songs we loved together - I just end up crying and shutting down. 

It feels impossible to do anything "for her" without being swallowed by grief all over again. Maybe I'm not strong enough yet.
therapist:
I hear how overwhelming it feels to try honoring her through actions right now - like the grief becomes too much to bear in those moments. Your voice sounds both tender and determined as you talk about this, showing how much you want to find ways to stay connected to her.  

What if we started with something very small, perhaps just a minute or two with those songs, allowing the tears to come without judging yourself for them? Would that feel manageable to try?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
